# Getting Started with Python and PyCharm

This guide will walk you through setting up Python and Pycharm on your personal computer.

**Sections:**

* [Installing Python and PyCharm on your own computer](#installing-python-and-pycharm-on-your-own-computer)
* [Starting up PyCharm the first time](#starting-up-pycharm-the-first-time)
* [Setting up a new project](#setting-up-a-new-project)
* [Creating a Python file](#creating-a-python-file)

---

# Installing Python and PyCharm on your own computer {#installing-python-and-pycharm-on-your-own-computer}

## **Download and Install Python**

Your first step is to download a Python interpreter from the Python website. Your computer may have Python installed on it already, but it is probably good to get an updated version.

Go to the [Python Downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/) page. Download the current version. Be sure to check that you are downloading an installer that is correct for your operating system, and pay attention to the difference between 32-bit and 64-bit computers when choosing an installer.

Download the proper installer, and double-click on it to run it. Follow the instructions for the installer program.

## **Download and Install PyCharm**

Go to the [PyCharm website](https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/), select Download. Download the installer program and run it. Follow the installation instructions to install PyCharm.

# ---

# Starting up PyCharm the first time {#starting-up-pycharm-the-first-time}

Find the PyCharm application on your computer, and run it. The first time you run it, you may need to answer some questions to configure PyCharm. The screenshots below are for a Mac, your screens may look different on a Windows machine, but the questions should be essentially the same.

### **Accept terms**

If you are installing the PyCharm on your own computer, then you will see a page with JetBrains’ user agreement. Select the check box and then the Continue button.

![][image1]

### **PyCharm starting up**

If all goes well, PyCharm should then begin its startup process. You should see a screen like the following:

![][image2]

You may also see the “PyCharm Goes AI”  popup. Just close the popup; don’t click “Let’s Go”.

![][image3]

# ---

# Setting up a new project {#setting-up-a-new-project}

When you write Python programs with PyCharm, you must create a **project** to keep your code in.  You can think of a project as a folder where you put related code. Each project also remembers what Python interpreter should be used, and other special configurations.

You could decide to have one project for the whole semester, but that might get large and unwieldy. Instead, you could have a project called “Homework” where you keep all the code for homework assignments and one called “ICA” where you keep all your code for in-class assignments. Or you could make a project for each individual assignment. Just give them memorable names that don’t duplicate the name of a code file or Python module.

The first time you start up PyCharm, you will see a window like this:
![][image4]

Select “New Project”. If you don’t see the big New Project button, look on the left side for a “+ New…” button and use that. You will then be prompted to choose the location and name for the new project, and the version of Python to use with the project. **Warning: do not rush through the next window, the chances are good that the project interpreter will be wrong\!**

PyCharm will, by default, create a folder in your home directory called pythonProject, and it will put your projects there.  You can choose a different location and/or create a new file for your python projects.  **Then, before you click on the Create button**, look carefully at the second line, where it says “Interpreter type”

Pycharm will default to “Project venv”. **You do not want to do this.**  Instead, select “Custom environment” for “Interpreter type”. For the “Environment” make sure that “Select existing” is chosen.  The drop-down menu for “Type” should have “Python” selected.  The “Python path” may list Python interpreters, you want Python 3.13 (or whatever version you just downloaded). If it is not there, you can click on folder icon at the right to select the desired interpreter.

On a Mac, the Python interpreter is usually found in /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.13/bin/python3.13
or
/usr/local/bin/python3
On Windows, your installation may vary, but it is usually C:\\Users\\\<username\>\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python313/python.exe  Note that \<username\> should be replaced by your Windows username.

Once you create the project, you will get the most typical view of PyCharm: the project view. On the left you can see the project and any files or subfolders that are a part of it. On the right is the editor window, where you can create and edit programs. The bottom part of the window will display the results of running your code, or give you access to the Python Console.

![][image5]

## **Creating a Python Console**

The Python Console is a place to try out new commands and see how they work, and to have a conversation with Python where you type in commands and it immediately tells you what they do. To open a Python Console, click on the Python Console button in the lower left corner of the PyCharm window.

![][image6]

You can then type Python statements at the \>\>\> prompt.
![][image7]

## **Setting Preferences**

PyCharm has a boggling array of preferences you can set. First, let’s import the basic settings we need for COMP 123\.

* Download [this zip file](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1h-mD2sOOmGRyPZJrLmz4GvlAEH0WjNi9/view?usp=drive_link) and take note of where it gets saved.
* In PyCharm, navigate to File \> Manage IDE Settings \> Import Settings. Select that and find the comp123-pycharm-settings.zip file you just downloaded. Select it, then click Import and Restart.

Now let’s do a quick check on the settings you just imported and handle some that aren’t configured via the import. Navigate to File \> Settings.

Feel free to explore, but for now you might check out the Editor’s General Appearance preferences and add line numbers (PyCharm \-\> Settings \-\> Editor \-\> General \-\> Appearance), and make sure that “Show indent guides” is selected:
![][image8]

**Three changes you need to make are the following**:

1. Under Editor \-\> General \-\> Inline Completion uncheck the box that says “Enable local Full Line completion suggestions”.
2. Under Editor \-\> General \-\> Code Completion uncheck any of the boxes that are checked on this page.
3. Under Editor \-\> General \-\> Smart Keys uncheck the boxes for “Insert paired brackets” and “Insert pair quote”

You can change the colors used in the editor by looking under Appearance & Behavior \-\> Appearance.  Here you can set the theme.  Some people prefer a light theme while others prefer dark.  Feel free to explore\!

# ---

# Creating a Python File {#creating-a-python-file}

Once you have created a project, you can create a Python code file by selecting “New File or Directory…” from the File menu. A menu will appear; select “Python File”. PyCharm will ask for the file name, and then make the file ready for you to edit.
![][image9]

Once you have a file created you should see the file name appear in the left window under the project name.  The file can be edited in the right editor window.
![][image10]

To run a Python code file for the first time, you can either select Run… from the Run menu or, if you have an editor window open for the file, you may right-click on the blank space in the editor window and select Run \<filename\> from there. A Run window should appear at the bottom of the window. Controls for stopping and re-running the program appear at the left edge of the Run window. After the first run, you can re-run the program using the methods already described, or by clicking on the green arrow at the left edge of the Run window, **or** by clicking on the green arrow in the upper right corner of the whole window.

# ---

# Creating a new Python Project

You probably don’t want to put all of your python files into the same project.  To create a new python project after your first, select “New Project…” under the File menu.  This will take you back to this new Project window.

You will need to enter a new name for your project in the “Location” box.
Again, you do NOT want the “Interpreter type” to be “Project venv”.  Switch the “Interpreter type” to “Custom environment”.  Then make sure “Environment” has “Select existing” selected.  “Type” should have “Python” selected from the dropdown menu.  And the “Python path” should have “Python 3.13” selected.  Since you have already done this once, it should know where python is, but if not, see instructions above on how to find “Python 3.13” on your machine if it’s not an option from the drop down menu.

Then click the “Create” button in the bottom right corner.
A pop-up window may appear asking how you want to Open the new project.  If you select “This Window” it will replace the current project you are working on.  If you select “New Window” it will open a second Pycharm window with the new project.
